strengths: Structural conservation guarantee via Proposition 1 is elegant and rigorously proven; conservation errors reach machine precision (~10^-8), a clear practical advantage over soft-constraint methods
Comprehensive theoretical framework with hard lower-bound guarantees (L-head) and effective dual-bound control via DCL (D-head); clear proofs in appendix
Thorough experimental validation across four diverse benchmarks (convection-diffusion, shallow water, traffic flow, spinodal decomposition) spanning different physics and constraint types
Strong empirical results: 17.3× speedup on spinodal decomposition, 67% reduction in shallow water depth MAE vs projection baselines, preservation of microstructural statistics beyond training horizon

Rigorous design validation through extensive ablations (Tables 6-7) demonstrating importance of each component; ERF analysis (Figures 4, 12-13) convincingly shows learned operators are genuinely local
Honest limitations discussion and transparent reporting of D-head violations as first-class metrics rather than hiding shortcomings; excellent scientific integrity
Clear presentation with logical flow; comprehensive appendix with complete proofs, experimental details, and supplementary visualizations
Configurable stencil radius enables large timesteps with localized effective receptive fields, achieving practical speedups while maintaining physical interpretation
weaknesses: D-head for dual-bounded quantities lacks strict theoretical guarantees; averaging Eq. (3) between outflow and inflow branches breaks both hard constraints, relying instead on empirical Dual Consistency Loss regularization (~0.5-7% violation rates). No convergence analysis provided for why DCL training works

Severe scope limitations: guarantees hold only for periodic boundary conditions (Dirichlet/Neumann/mixed BCs require unspecified 'careful treatment'); restricted to source-free conservation laws; limited to regular grids, excluding unstructured meshes and adaptive refinement—critical for modern scientific computing applications

No direct experimental comparison to FINN (Praditia et al., 2021), the most closely related flux-based method, making it difficult to assess the actual advantage of the proposed approach over existing flux-based surrogates

Incremental methodological novelty: flux-based conservation is established; main contributions are specific parameterizations (L/U/D-heads) and stencil channelization from LBM. While integration is sensible, the advance is evolutionary rather than revolutionary

Practical limitations: stencil radius must be manually tuned for each timestep (Table 5 shows different radii needed for different ∆t values); no principled or adaptive mechanism provided. Task-specific FluxNet-LAP for shallow water (momentum decomposition with h² pressure gating) introduces manually-designed physics, somewhat contradicting the generic framework claim

Small datasets for some benchmarks: 100 training trajectories for traffic flow; single long trajectory for spinodal decomposition using one-shot learning paradigm. Generalization to larger, more diverse datasets or harder problems unclear
Limited analysis of failure modes, hyperparameter sensitivity (e.g., DCL weight γ), or performance on problems with strong nonlinearities beyond traffic flow shocks
Number of random seeds for error bars not explicitly stated; no explicit code availability statement limiting reproducibility despite detailed documentation

strengths: Rigorous mathematical treatment with formal propositions and complete proofs for conservation (Prop. 1) and hard bound guarantees (Props. 2-3)
Comprehensive four-benchmark evaluation spanning diverse physics (convection-diffusion, shallow water, traffic, spinodal decomposition) with multiple evaluation metrics beyond MAE
Achieves machine-precision conservation (10^-7 to 10^-8 level) and strong empirical bound satisfaction; 17.3× speedup on spinodal decomposition while preserving two-point correlation statistics
Clear problem motivation and well-written exposition; honest limitations discussion acknowledging that D-head lacks strict dual-bound guarantees and that periodic boundaries are required
Detailed ablation studies (Tables 6-7) demonstrating importance of design choices (L-head for positivity, h² gating, DCL for dual bounds)
weaknesses: Limited novelty over flux-based methods: FINN (Praditia et al., 2021) already learns flux functions respecting conservation. The bound parameterization (sigmoid for outflow %, softmax for distribution) is a straightforward extension rather than conceptual advance. No direct experimental comparison with FINN provided.

D-head lacks theoretical guarantees despite being central for dual-bounded problems: averaging two branches with soft Dual Consistency Loss (Eq. 3-4) is inelegant, empirical violation rates reach 2.41% (Table 7), and paper doesn't pursue principled alternatives (e.g., feasible projection).

Severe applicability limitations from periodic boundary condition requirement: all proofs require periodic BC; extension to Dirichlet/Neumann/mixed boundaries is unaddressed. Cannot handle unstructured meshes or source terms. These assumptions eliminate many real-world applications.

Weak experimental setup: (1) Missing direct comparison with FINN despite being most relevant prior work; (2) FNO baseline appears standard without recent improvements; (3) max training grid 128×128 (downsampled from larger); (4) soft constraint penalty treated as strawman without exploring sophisticated alternatives; (5) only 4 problem classes.

Problem-specific design choices reduce generality: FluxNet-LAP (shallow water specialization with h² gating) is ad-hoc, generalization to other coupled systems unclear, and ablation (Table 6) shows marginal benefit. Stencil radius must be manually tuned per timestep with no adaptive scheduling.

Incomplete experimental analysis: no sample efficiency study despite expensive label generation, no wall-clock training time comparison, pushforward training shown marginal in ablations (Table 6) despite being universal in experiments, ERF analysis shallow without deep dive into learning dynamics implications.

Technical concerns with D-head design: (1) Averaging branches (Eq. 3) can violate both bounds if branches disagree despite DCL; (2) DCL hyperparameter γ requires tuning with no guidance; (3) theoretical guarantee asymmetry undermines claim of 'structural' constraint enforcement.

Missing key related work and comparisons: no discussion of constraint learning in neural networks, recent entropy-stable methods (Liu et al., 2025), or hybrid symbolic-numeric approaches. Should compare with FINN quantitatively on same benchmarks.

strengths: Novel flux-based parameterization: Shifting from state prediction to feasible transport operators is elegant and addresses the core problem of conservation drift and bound violations through architectural design

Solid theoretical contributions: Propositions 1-3 cleanly establish machine-precision conservation and hard structural guarantees for single-sided bounds (L/U-heads), with proofs that are mathematically correct

Comprehensive experimental validation: Four diverse benchmarks (convection-diffusion, shallow water, traffic flow, spinodal decomposition) with proper baselines, ablations, multiple metrics, and demonstration of long-horizon stability
Practical impact: Achieves 17.3× speedup on spinodal decomposition while maintaining accuracy and statistical fidelity; machine-precision conservation enables stable long-rollout predictions
Rigorous methodology: Proper use of pushforward training, effective receptive field analysis confirming local transport behavior, statistical preservation metrics beyond pointwise accuracy
Honest limitations discussion: Transparent about D-head empiricism, boundary condition restrictions, and scope limitations; does not overstate claims
Strong presentation: Clear motivation, well-organized method section, informative tables and figures, extensive proofs and supplementary experiments in appendix
weaknesses: D-head lacks theoretical guarantees: Dual-bounded case relies on Dual Consistency Loss (DCL) for empirical agreement between branches (~0.5-7% violation rates); averaging two branches breaks structural guarantees unless perfect agreement

Limited scope: Restricted to periodic boundaries (extension to Dirichlet/Neumann stated as future work), source-free conservation laws only, and regular grids—limits applicability to real-world problems
Fixed stencil neighborhood requires tuning: No principled methodology for selecting radius for new problems; must be tuned separately for each timestep, and no adaptive strategies explored

Incomplete baseline analysis: Projection method implementation details not fully specified (especially for coupled momentum in shallow water); soft constraint baselines use simple penalties; no comparison with recent methods like PDE-Refiner
D-head design choices underjustified: Why average two branches rather than select? DCL weight γ lacks sensitivity analysis; design motivations compared to alternatives not explored
Statistical quantification gaps: Error bars provided only for MAE; conservation error and violation rates lack uncertainty quantification; no significance testing between methods
Limited analysis of failure modes: Unclear when/why method might fail under distributional shift; D-head empiricism creates risk in demanding applications with strict constraint requirements
